metadata.title: What the Remotion Skills Do
metadata.audience: Bear and toolkit users: what the installed Remotion agent skills do, shown running
metadata.source_doc: github.com/remotion-dev/skills v4.0.534, installed 2026-10-10 into brutalist.art/runtime/remotion/.agents/skills; the rules demonstrated in this toolkit's own Remotion 4.0.534 project

beats.narration_text: Hey Claude. I just installed Remotion's own agent skills into the brutalist toolkit. What do they actually do, and what do they let the toolkit do that it couldn't before?

props.command: Hey Claude. I just installed Remotion's own agent skills into the brutalist toolkit. What do they actually do, and what do they let the toolkit do that it couldn't before?

beats.narration_text: Sawubona. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. These skills are not a plugin that renders anything. They are fifty short rule files that load into an agent, mine included, when it writes Remotion code, so the code it writes is the current, correct way: frame-driven motion, timing on the node, premounted media, measured text, captions as data. This film shows each rule running for real in the brutalist toolkit, and then the three things that needed a newer Remotion, now rendered live.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: What a skill is. One command inside the Remotion project installs them: seven folders under dot agents slash skills, and a symlink from dot claude slash skills so Claude Code finds them. A lockfile records the exact version, so an update never changes the rules halfway through a film.
beats.motion_claim: Real commands and their real output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Open one. A skill is a markdown file with a name, a version, and rules. The markup skill opens with the two that matter most: take the frame rate from the video config and keep timing on the J S X node, and drive every animation from the current frame. A C S S transition will not render. The router skill sends an agent to the right file for the task.

props.title: zsh — brutalist.art/runtime/remotion
lines: description: Content, animation and effects best practices
Inside a composition or scene component, get `fps` from
CSS `transition` or `animation` will not render correctly …

beats.motion_claim: Real commands and their real output land in order.

beats.narration_text: The first rule, shown. Two boxes are told to slide across the stage. The left one uses a C S S transition. The right one uses interpolate over the current frame. Remotion renders one frame at a time, as a screenshot, so a C S S transition never gets its two seconds: the left box teleports to the end in a single frame and sits there. The right box moves, and lands in the same place in every render. That is the whole reason for the rule.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Easing. Four dots travel the same distance in the same time. Linear is mechanical. The bezier the skills recommend, point one six, one, point three, one, arrives fast and settles. A spring with heavy damping pushes with no bounce. And the last pair shows scale: the same growth looks slow at the end unless you ask for perceptual scale, which the skills now call out.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Sequencing. A series lays clips end to end, and the skills say: premount every timed item one second early, with premount for equal to the frame rate, so media and fonts are ready before the cut. Watch the ruler: the grey band before each clip is the premount, the playhead crosses it, and the clip is already there when its turn comes.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Transitions. The transitions package gives a transition series with fade, slide and wipe between scenes, and the skills explain the trap: a transition overlaps its neighbours, so the composition is shorter than the sum of its scenes, and you subtract the overlap when you compute the length. Three cards, three cuts, and the running frame count shows the overlap.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Measuring text. The layout utilities measure a string in its real font before it is placed. The left box sets a long title at one size and clips it. The right box asks fit text for the largest size that fits the width, and shows the size it found. For this toolkit that is the difference between catching a truncated title in a gate and never producing one.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Captions as data. The captions package parses a subtitle file into caption objects with start and end times in milliseconds. This is a real caption file, from the first film in the Northeastern research computing series, and these are its first cues, drawn as pages, each word lighting on its own time. The toolkit already writes these files; now a composition can read them.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Audio visualization. The media utilities read the waveform of an audio file and give a spectrum per frame. These bars are this sentence: my own narration, analysed as it plays, nothing faked. Bass on the left, treble on the right, and the shape follows the voice.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Media. The multimedia skill reads a file's duration with the media bunny library instead of shelling out to F F probe. Here it measures the opening card of that same research computing film: twelve point five two eight seconds, where F F probe says twelve point four eight, the gap being how each counts the last M P three frame. The toolkit's clock stays in Python, but a composition can now size itself from the audio it plays.
beats.motion_claim: Real commands and their real output land in order.

beats.narration_text: Render. The render skill is the command line: render, still, and a frames mode that writes several frames as images in one call, which is exactly how this toolkit's gates sample a beat. It also documents transparent output: P N G frames, an alpha pixel format, Pro Res four four four four or V P nine, for a clip that drops onto another video with no background.

$ npx remotion still Root.tsx SkillDemo frame.png --frame=45
$ npx remotion render Root.tsx SkillDemo out/ \
$ npx remotion render Root.tsx Logo out.mov --image-format=png \

beats.motion_claim: Real commands and their real output land in order.

beats.narration_text: And the toolkit already renders every card this way: the writing quill from the previous film, rendered as a still with alpha, sits on a kraft checkerboard with nothing behind it. That is the same render path, with the flags the skill names.

show.event: the alpha still lands on the checker

beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Now the part that needed the upgrade. Three of the rules describe features newer than the Remotion this toolkit was running. So the toolkit moved from four point oh point four eight six to the latest, four point oh point five three four, every Remotion package at once, as the upgrade skill says. React went to nineteen with it, because the new transitions build carries React nineteen inside. Then every composition was re-rendered, and the effects, highlights and blur below are real renders, not captures.
beats.motion_claim: Real commands and their real output land in order.

beats.narration_text: First, effects: an effects array on images, video and solids, drawn by the graphics card. Here is one portrait of Professor Bear, four ways: grayscale, duotone in the toolkit's own ink and kraft, a terracotta halftone, and a vignette with roughened edges. Each is one line, driven by the frame, and the documentary still treatment the toolkit used to build by hand is now exactly that.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Second, text highlights: hand-drawn circles, highlights, underlines, strike-throughs and boxes, each a component driven by a progress value from the frame. The terracotta ring this toolkit used to draw by hand in every scene is now a Circle around a word.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Third, motion blur. The top card is a hard-edged move, every frame sharp. The bottom is wrapped in camera motion blur, which renders each frame at twelve moments inside a two-hundred-and-forty-degree shutter and averages them, so the card smears the way a real camera sees it. The newer H T M L in canvas blur needs a Chrome flag, so this is the component that runs everywhere.
beats.motion_claim: A live Remotion composition demonstrates the rule.

beats.narration_text: Keeping it current. The skills come from a public repository, and one command pulls updates. The lockfile changes with them, so the update is a diff you can read before the next film, and a commit you can roll back. The old snapshot in the toolkit's docs folder now points at the live set.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The skills are rule files an agent reads while it writes Remotion code, not a renderer. The rules that matter: frame-driven motion, timing on the node, premount a second early, measure text before placing it. They are installed at a pinned version, with transitions, layout utilities, captions and media utilities added to match. Captions and audio become data a composition can read, while the toolkit's clock stays in Python. The toolkit then upgraded to the latest Remotion, with React nineteen, and effects, text highlights and motion blur now render live. And an update is a command and a diff.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: In my Remotion project, read the installed remotion-markup skill and audit this component: [paste one component]. List every place it breaks a rule, such as CSS transitions, transform strings, missing premountFor, timing not derived from fps, or unmeasured text, and rewrite only those lines. Then check two things yourself. Render three frames with the frames flag and look at them: does anything still animate by C S S? And did it change only the lines it named?
